blogs.title: Red Lines and Red Flags: The Federal Circuit Tosses the ’134 Verdict over an Expert’s Muddled Mapping
blogs.description: The panel reversed on the ’134 patent because Finesse’s expert repeatedly mapped the claim-required “interference generating signals” to a modeled PIM path created downstream of the RF ADC—i.e., after sampling—making it impossible for the receiver to have sampled those signals as claim 1[a] requires. The district court tried to salvage the verdict by inferring the expert meant x1 and x2 instead, but the Federal Circuit found his testimony self-contradictory and unclear, invoking Johns Hopkins v. Datascope to reject verdicts built on such pivots. This post unpacks the evidentiary gap, the court’s insistence on a clean, element-by-element mapping, and the practical lesson: experts who lean on block-diagram legends and then “clarify” at trial risk losing under substantial-evidence review.

blogs.title: Seven Means Seven: Why the ’775 Patent Failed on Proof, Not Construction
blogs.description: Although the court declined to find a prosecution-history surrender that would limit “three signals S1, S2, S3” to three unique inputs, it still reversed because Finesse didn’t prove the seven specific third-order multiplications the claim requires. The Nokia documents showed only three distinct multiplications—and involved modulus and complex conjugates—not a set that could be cleanly mapped to the seven claimed products. Attempts on appeal to retrofit the mapping with a ten-term polynomial went nowhere because the record lacked a jury-ready explanation. We explore how this ruling threads the needle on claim scope (separately identifiable vs. unique) while demanding precise mathematical proof of each recited operation.

blogs.title: Substantial Evidence, Fifth-Circuit Style: Undoing a $166 Million E.D. Tex. Verdict
blogs.description: The Federal Circuit reviewed the denial of JMOL under Fifth Circuit standards and the infringement findings for substantial evidence, ultimately concluding no reasonable jury could find for Finesse on either patent. This post analyzes the procedural architecture: preserving Rule 50 issues; how regional-circuit JMOL standards intersect with Federal Circuit substantial-evidence review; and the court’s skepticism toward inferential fixes for trial testimony gaps. We also flag practice pointers for patent trials in E.D. Tex.: lock down your expert mappings to claim elements and ensure the record stands on its own without post-verdict reconstruction.

blogs.title: After the Static: Implications for PIM-Cancellation Patents and Proving DSP Infringement
blogs.description: Vacating the lump-sum damages followed naturally from reversing infringement, but the broader signal to the industry is clearer: in DSP-heavy cases, plaintiffs must prove the math with rigor. For “sampling” limitations, ensure the accused path actually exists at the sampling point; for multiplication-based claims, walk the jury through each required operation and identity (including when modulus and complex conjugates are in play). The decision suggests patentees should draft with specificity about signal identities and operations—or risk losing to designs that use fewer unique inputs or different mathematical forms. Vendors deploying PIM-cancellation should note: internal block diagrams can be a double-edged sword if plaintiffs can’t convert them into element-by-element proof.
